transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Shaw (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Head of Platform), Miguel Rivera (Staff DevOps), Hana Kim (CTO)

Summary:
Quick demo of Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on prefetch/prefix KV caching and batching. Goal: show cost/latency tradeoffs for Sierra Sentinel's conversational agent workload, agree a small bench test and data share for precise sims.

Topics covered:
- Baseline: current per-request token counts, concurrency profile, SLAs
- Prefetch/prefix cache strategies and lookahead windows
- Batch sizing, concurrency, and autoscale interactions
- Cost model walkthrough (per-token, per-GPU hr assumptions, cache hit economics)
- Hosting options: hosted vs dedicated vs private and implications for PKI/KMS and audit logs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on the account. Marcus our SE will walk through the cost sims and prefetch ideas. Quick round robin intros?
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya here, head of platform at Sierra Sentinel, thinking about slashing token costs for our chat product while keeping 99th pct latency under 600ms.
[00:15] Miguel Rivera: Miguel, devops. I'll own the bench and infra bits.
[00:18] Hana Kim: Hana, CTO. Interested in tradeoffs and what falls over if we push prefetch too hard.
[00:22] Marcus Shaw: Marcus, Redwood SE, I did the econ sims we'll show. Note, some of the model names may be off in the transcript; our internal model is "redwood-compat-7B-q4" for the demo.
[00:33] Lena Park: Cool. High level: we want to save per-token cost using lookahead prefetch + prefix KV caching so you don't re-run long context repeatedly. Marcus, take it away.

[02:00] Marcus Shaw: Thanks. I put up a quick slide — imagine a conversational flow where the first N tokens (the prompt and system) are stable for session. With prefix cache we store the KV cache at the end of the system+few-turn context. On next calls we either reuse the cached KV or prefetch it asynchronously into the inference pod. That converts repeated compute of prefix into cheap memory reads.
[02:35] Miguel Rivera: Is this the same as session cache we tried with our on-prem LLM? We had issues with cache staleness when the prompt template changed.
[02:44] Marcus Shaw: Good point. Prefetch and prefix are complementary. Prefetch is proactive: when session activity shows a user likely to continue, we warm the KV on the serving node. Prefix cache is keyed to the exact prompt footprint — changes in template invalidates the key. We recommend a short template fingerprint in the key to control staleness.
[03:10] Priya Nair: What's a realistic hit rate? Our current app has a lot of small variations — names, slot fillers, but the system and instruction text is stable.
[03:20] Marcus Shaw: In similar customers we've seen 45-70% effective hit rate on the long system/prompt portion with a 10-20 token difference tolerance, if you do a two-tier key: template fingerprint + normalized entity placeholders. But if you have heavy personalization, hit rate drops.
[04:05] Lena Park: We're going to show a cost sim with conservative 40% hit, and an optimistic 65% hit so you can see sensitivity.

[05:00] Marcus Shaw: Alright cost model layout: tokens broken into prefix (system+few turns), input tokens, and gen tokens. Baseline for Sierra is ~420 input tokens avg per request and 300 generation tokens — total 720 tokens. Baseline concurrency 60 qps sustained with spikes to 150. Your current hosted spend estimate you shared was $22k/month on 3rd-party API — correct?
[05:35] Priya Nair: Roughly. That includes embeddings and some heavy pipelines, but chat is the big driver.
[05:40] Marcus Shaw: For the sim I used our redwood-compat-7B-q4 perf numbers: uncached per-token compute cost equivalent and throughput per GPU at 1500 tokens/sec for typical prompt length. With prefix caching at 50% hit you save about 30-40% on per-request infer compute. Prefetch moves some of the warm latency out of the tail by warming the cache before the next request.
[06:15] Miguel Rivera: So prefetch reduces cold-start latency but prefetching too aggressively increases wasted GPU time?
[06:22] Marcus Shaw: Exactly. Prefetch policy is tuned by lookahead probability — we estimate session continuation probability from your session telemetry. Policy threshold trades off wasted prefetch ops vs tail reduction. In the workbook we'll show a curve and you can pick an operating point.

[07:00] Hana Kim: Walk me through a concrete scenario: user completes turn A then B then C, what's hit rate and latency with and without prefetch?
[07:10] Marcus Shaw: Without cache: full prefix recompute every turn. Let's say baseline 420 prefix tokens cost X ms. With prefix cache hit: you only compute new input+gen tokens so latency drops by roughly the prefix compute fraction. With prefetch on turn B about to predict C you asynchronously load KV so when the request arrives for C the pod already has warmed KV — tail 95th reduces by 40-60ms in our sim, sometimes more for longer prefixes.
[08:00] Priya Nair: Can we approximate dollar numbers per 100k requests?
[08:05] Marcus Shaw: Yes. In the workbook sample: baseline compute cost for 100k requests = $1,900 (numbers illustrative) on hosted API. With 50% prefix hit and moderate prefetch policy we estimate $1,250 — about 35% savings. With 65% hit it goes to $1,050. These assume no change in embedding or other pipelines.
[08:30] Miguel Rivera: Those are big savings. But how does concurrency factor? If we fold batching and higher concurrency, do we need fewer GPUs?
[08:40] Marcus Shaw: Batching helps a lot for throughput-optimized workloads. For interactive low-latency you trade batch size for latency. Our recommend policy is continuous batching with a 20-40ms max batching wait for typical chat. In throughput mode (async background jobs) you can batch up more and reduce p50 cost. For your 60 qps sustained, careful batching + prefix hit can reduce required GPUs by ~25% in our sim.

[09:30] Priya Nair: Any differences between hosted Redwood and Dedicated for this strategy?
[09:36] Marcus Shaw: Mechanically, same runtime features in hosted and Dedicated. Difference is isolation and reserved capacity. Dedicated gives you pinned GPUs which are better when your traffic is predictable and you want to run aggressive prefetches without noisy neighbor effects. Hosted gives elastic capacity but prefetch policies might be constrained by ephemeral pod lifetimes — we handle warming via ephemeral prefetch agents but latency patterns differ. We'll put a comparative appendix in the workbook.
[10:10] Miguel Rivera: For private on-prem, does the KV cache lifetime live only in GPU memory? What's persisted?
[10:16] Marcus Shaw: KV typically lives in GPU memory for speed. We can persist to local SSD for warm restarts; in private deployments we can expose options to checkpoint KV to a Redis-like store if you want long-lived sessionization. That increases engineering complexity.

[11:00] Hana Kim: Security: if we cache session content, how do we avoid retaining PII?
[11:05] Lena Park: Good question. We recommend deterministic redaction before caching (strip PII, replace with pseudotokens) or use short TTLs and encrypt KVs at rest with your KMS in Private/Dedicated. We also support audit logs for cache reads/writes. 
[11:22] Priya Nair: Is that part of SOC2 docs?
[11:25] Lena Park: Yes, our security pack covers data flows, encryption, and audit controls. We'll attach it.

[12:00] Marcus Shaw: Back to economics. I'll show the spreadsheet screenshot — sorry for the rough transcript in the auto-export, the numbers are: baseline tokens per month: 1.9B, baseline compute cost $42k. With a 40% prefix hit and tuned batching we model $26k. Lookahead prefetch adds an ops cost of about $1.2k but reduces tail latency enough to hit your 600ms 99th target.
[12:45] Miguel Rivera: Pre-calc: what's the CPU/network overhead for prefetch?
[12:50] Marcus Shaw: Prefetch ops are smaller than full inference but you still incur model memory IO; network cost depends on warm strategy. If we prefetch into the same pod it's local, minimal network. If the warm cache is served from a cache tier it's more networky. We'll detail both in the workbook.

[14:10] Priya Nair: In terms of rollout, we'd want a canary: maybe 10% of sessions with prefix/prefetch, compare latency and costs. How quickly can we iterate?
[14:18] Lena Park: You can do a canary within days. For Dedicated we can provision a small pool overnight; for Hosted we can toggle policies per-customer. We'll help set up a canary and the dashboards (per-route cost & latency).

[15:00] Marcus Shaw: One more demo fragment — console screenshot showing Optimize recommendations: recommended batch target 16 tokens, max batch wait 30ms, prefetch lookahead 0.6 probability, prefix TTL 1800s. These are starting points.
[15:25] Hana Kim: If we autoscale aggressively, does prefetch cause a lot of spiky GPU utilization?
[15:30] Marcus Shaw: Prefetch can cause spikey patterns if your policy is naive. We recommend smoothing via quota on prefetch per pod and a backoff when pod utilization hits threshold. Also prefetch is typically cheaper than full inference — still important to monitor.

[16:20] Miguel Rivera: Bench test specifics? What metrics should we collect?
[16:24] Marcus Shaw: Collect per-request token counts, prefix hit flag, latency p50/p90/p99, GPU utilization, average batch sizes, and prefetch success/waste rates. We'll provide a bench harness we use internally.

[17:15] Priya Nair: Are there any edge cases where this backfires?
[17:18] Marcus Shaw: Yes — very high personalization (unique system tokens per user), and very short sessions where prefix is tiny. Also when session churn is high and prefetch is overly aggressive, wasted ops can neutralize savings. We'll include guardrails and a monitoring playbook.

[18:05] Lena Park: Quick commercial note: typical pilot terms are 6-8 weeks with a shared cost workbook and a small committed bench. We'll put a proposal in the follow-up email.

[19:00] Hana Kim: Ok good. Can you also include an example of request normalization (how to build template fingerprints)? Our engineering team wants a pattern.
[19:07] Marcus Shaw: Yes we'll attach a short example code snippet for normalization, placeholder substitution and how to compute keys.

[20:10] Priya Nair: Anything else we should know about monitoring?
[20:12] Marcus Shaw: Our Console exposes per-route cost, per-token breakdown, and a prefetch dashboard with wasted prefetches over time. Alerts can be configured for prefetch waste > 20% or p99 latency regressions.

[21:00] Lena Park: Wrap-up recap coming from me in the notes: 1) Redwood to share workbook + security pack, 2) Sierra to share traffic histogram and prompt set, 3) schedule bench run. Any final questions?
[21:12] Miguel Rivera: One small one — license terms if we go Dedicated vs Hosted?
[21:17] Lena Park: Pricing differs; Dedicated has reservation commitments and different overage math. I'll include a short pricing comparison table.
[21:30] Hana Kim: Great, thanks.
[21:35] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the attachments and proposed bench slots.

End of transcript.
